title: France's Open-Air Incinerators: The Uncounted Toxic Toll Of Annual Street Protests
desc:
France's Open-Air Incinerators: The Uncounted Toxic Toll Of Annual Street Protests

Every time political anger spills into French streets - whether over pension reforms, fuel taxes, police shootings, or the annual ritual of Saint-Sylvestre on New Year's Eve - the post-mortem follows a familiar script. The Ministry of the Interior tallies the arrests, insurers calculate the millions in property damage, and municipal crews sweep up the melted asphalt before morning commuters arrive. The rioters - who kicked this off in working-class banlieues (which has high concentrations of North African and sub-Saharan immigrants) are burning whatever they can get their hands on; cars, tires, plastic bins, buildings, etc.

And, as one might imagine, this is extremely toxic.

Over the past decade, an average of 35,000 to 40,000 vehicles have been intentionally torched across France every year, punctuated by massive spasms of civil unrest - such as the June 2023 riots, which saw more than 12,000 vehicles burned, or New Year's Eve 2025/2026, when 1,173 parked vehicles were reduced to ash overnight. When you strip away the political theater, France's recurring protests function as unlicensed, open-air hazardous waste incinerators operating at breathing height in the country's most densely populated neighborhoods.

In the European Union, an industrial waste incinerator is legally required to burn materials above 850°C inside sealed chambers equipped with rapid gas-quenching towers and multi-stage chemical scrubbers. A burning Peugeot or stuffed municipal dumpster on a narrow street in Paris, Lyon, or Marseille smolders in an oxygen-starved state between 250°C and 450°C - the exact temperature sweet spot for cooking up some of the deadliest carcinogens and "forever chemicals" known to science.

Unlike a wildfire, whose immense heat lofts smoke miles into the sky, a street fire has a weak heat plume that gets trapped between mid-rise apartment blocks. Caught in street-level wind tunnels, the smoke pools for hours. Within 50 meters (164 feet), it delivers a choking, acidic shock; out to 300 meters, it seeps through apartment window air vents (bouches d'aération) from the ground floor to the sixth story, coating balconies, playgrounds, and parks in oily black fallout; out to several kilometers, it merges into a toxic citywide haze.

The result is a slow-motion public and ecological health crisis - one that poisons residents, first responders, family pets, and urban wildlife long after the flames are put out.

Tires

A standard set of four passenger car tires contains nearly 90 pounds (40 kilograms) of synthetic petroleum-based rubber, heavy industrial oils, and chemical preservatives added to keep tires from cracking in the sun and street air. Stacking tires onto protest barricades or burning them on a car axle is essentially lighting a barrel of crude oil mixed with rubber cement in the middle of a residential street.

Because open tire fires burn poorly, they pump out thick, oily black clouds packed with Benzo[a]pyrene - the same cancer-causing tar found in cigarette smoke and chimney soot - alongside 1,3-butadiene (an industrial gas used to manufacture synthetic rubber, carpet backing, and shoe soles) and 6PPD-quinone (a toxic byproduct created when tire rubber preservatives react with the air). Pound for pound, a burning tire releases up to 1,000 times more cancer-causing tar than the tailpipe of a modern car.

EFFECT ON HUMANS & ANIMALS: Benzo[a]pyrene is a top-tier human carcinogen. Once breathed in on fine soot or absorbed through the skin, the body converts it into compounds that permanently damage DNA and switch off the body's natural tumor-fighting genes, driving lung and bladder cancers, while 1,3-butadiene attacks bone marrow to trigger leukemia. Because heavy tire soot settles onto sidewalks and grass within 50 to 300 meters and sticks around for months, neighborhood dogs, cats, and ground-feeding birds continuously swallow and inhale toxic doses through their paws, fur, and feathers. A 2026 study by researchers at York University and Environment and Climate Change Canada (Environment International) found that airborne tire preservatives break down into chemical cocktails that trigger aggressive inflammation in human immune cells in the lungs. Recent toxicological research on human liver cells and 2026 studies in Environmental Science & Technology showed that tire-derived 6PPD-quinone damages human liver tissue and causes mass die-offs in fish when rainwater washes street runoff into local rivers - though French public health agencies still have not officially linked urban tire-fire hotspots with local cancer or veterinary illness spikes.

Cars (Seats, Dashboards & Wiring)

A modern car is built with 250 to 350 kilograms of plastics, foams, and synthetic fabrics. The seat cushions are made of polyurethane foam - the same spongy material inside living-room couches and memory-foam mattresses - while the miles of electrical wiring behind the dashboard are wrapped in PVC (the same chlorinated plastic used to make household plumbing pipes, vinyl window frames, and shower curtains).

When a car is torched, the smoldering seat cushions vent lethal clouds of hydrogen cyanide - the same chemical released by the World War II poison gas Zyklon B - while the melting PVC wiring reacts with the copper wires inside it to cook up chlorinated dioxins and furans, the infamous class of ultra-toxic "forever chemicals" found in Agent Orange. According to European emission inventory figures and Germany's official tailpipe inventory factors, torching a single car releases about 0.048 mg of dioxins and furans (in toxic equivalents) - as much as an ordinary passenger car would emit driving roughly 8 million kilometers, or 200 laps around the Earth's equator.

EFFECT ON HUMANS & ANIMALS: Within 50 meters of a burning car, cyanide gas and airborne hydrochloric acid (a harsh, corrosive acid used in industrial concrete cleaners and swimming pool treatments) burn the airways and starve the heart and brain of oxygen. Further out, dioxins settle into neighborhood dirt and courtyard dust, where they take 10 to 25 years to break down. Once inside the human body, dioxins lock into body fat and liver tissue - the body needs 7 to 11 years to clear even half of them - scrambling hormones, promoting cancer, and crossing the placenta to stunt fetal growth. Paris-region soil is already so heavily contaminated that, after a 2023 study prompted by concerns over the Ivry waste incinerator found dioxins, PCBs and PFAS in backyard eggs across the capital and its inner suburbs, the Regional Health Agency (ARS) of Île-de-France warned residents of the roughly 400 communes of the greater Paris area not to eat eggs from their own hens [1]. The agency tied the contamination to dense, long-industrialized urban soil rather than any single source - and every torched car adds straight to that toxic soil bank. Research led by Inserm and Université Paris Cité has shown how prenatal exposure to urban air pollution damages the placenta and harms fetal development, while a 2024 French Senate investigation and ANSES occupational risk reports documented surging rates of bladder, prostate, and blood cancers among French firefighters (sapeurs-pompiers) routinely exposed to urban fire smoke - even as high civilian cancer and infant mortality rates in arson-heavy suburbs like Seine-Saint-Denis remain officially blamed on highway traffic rather than recurring street fires [2].

Electric & Hybrid Vehicles (Lithium-Ion Batteries)

As France's car fleet goes electric, street arson has acquired a nasty new chemical edge. An electric vehicle's battery pack is essentially a giant, thousand-pound version of the rechargeable battery in a smartphone or laptop, packed with chemical fluids that carry electric charge and hundreds of pounds of mined metals.

When a lithium-ion battery catches fire and enters "thermal runaway" - an unstoppable, self-feeding chemical meltdown - its internal battery fluids vaporize into clouds of corrosive hydrogen fluoride gas (a tissue-eating industrial acid used to etch glass and strip rust off stainless steel) alongside invisible metallic dust made of cobalt, nickel, manganese, lithium, and antimony (heavy metals used in industrial alloys, magnets, and ammunition). Putting out a single burning EV takes up to 30,000 liters of water - roughly ten times more than a gas-powered car - turning city streets into rivers of toxic metallic runoff.

EFFECT ON HUMANS & ANIMALS: Hydrogen fluoride gas passes straight through the lungs and skin into the bloodstream, where it strips vital calcium and magnesium out of the body - a chemical reaction that can trigger fluid in the lungs, permanent airway scarring, and cardiac arrest. Meanwhile, heavy metals never break down in nature; they stay in urban dirt and river mud forever, poisoning earthworms, insects, and the city songbirds that feed on them. A November 2025 Fire Safety Research Institute (FSRI), NIOSH, and Duke University study and a February 2026 FSRI follow-up study confirmed that burning EVs release substantially higher airborne levels of corrosive fluoride and heavy metals than gas vehicles, and that chemicals in vehicle fire smoke have a higher potential to cause genetic mutations in bacterial tests than smoke from burning wood, household trash, or crude oil. Furthermore, a September 2026 CDC/NIOSH investigation found that California firefighters who breathed battery fumes for just seconds to five minutes while cleaning up a crashed Tesla - with no flames even visible - suffered lasting lung injuries. One firefighter required oxygen after his blood oxygen plunged to 86% just from walking, four developed new high blood pressure within a month, and four were still unable to work about 11 months later - an acute toxic hazard that France's fixed city air monitors cannot even detect on riot nights.

Plastic Dumpsters & Barricades

The signature fuel of French street protests is the green 660-liter wheeled municipal dumpster. The bin itself is molded from thick HDPE plastic - the same heavy-duty plastic used to make milk jugs, laundry detergent bottles, and plastic patio furniture - and is typically stuffed with household trash, old electronics coated in chemical flame-retardants, and treated construction lumber.

Melting and burning thousands of these giant plastic vats on the pavement releases concentrated fumes of benzene (a toxic petrochemical solvent found in gasoline, paint strippers, and industrial glues), formaldehyde (the pungent preservative used in embalming fluid and pressed plywood), and brominated furans (toxic cousins of dioxin formed when flame-retardant electronics burn). Worse, these chemicals hitch a ride on ultrafine soot - microscopic specks of carbon 1,000 times thinner than a human hair.

title: Why Can Nothing Be Built In Britain?
desc:
Why Can Nothing Be Built In Britain?

Authored by Mani Basharzad via The Foundation for Economic Education,

A public company in the UK was building a high-speed railway when it suddenly faced a regulation that few could have predicted: a £100 million ($132 million) bat tunnel.

The railway passed through Sheephouse Wood, an area inhabited by rare Bechstein’s bats. To comply with environmental regulations that protect the bats from colliding with high-speed trains, the company had to build a roughly one-kilometer covered structure alongside the railway. This structure has since become widely known in the UK as the “bat tunnel.”

If you think this is just one case, let me tell you about the fish disco.

EDF Energy was developing a new nuclear power station in Somerset, which draws cooling water from the Severn Estuary. The project faced regulatory requirements to reduce the number of fish being drawn into and killed by its cooling-water intake pipes. EDF agreed to three measures: specially designed low-velocity intake heads, a fish recovery-and-return system, and an acoustic fish deterrent—underwater speakers that make noise to steer fish away, nicknamed the “fish disco.” The acoustic deterrent alone reportedly costs about $66 million, while EDF says the full fish-protection package costs more than $926 million.

The problem with the UK is that it has become a vetocracy.

Francis Fukuyama, the famous author of “The End of History,” explored this problem in his often-overlooked book “ Political Order and Political Decay.” The concept helps explain part of the productivity puzzle in the Western world.

Vetocracy means “rule by veto”: a political system with so many points at which organized minorities, courts, agencies, legislators, or interest groups can block action that the majority struggles to govern.

At first glance, this might seem necessary to protect democracy from majority rule and dictatorship. The separation of powers, independent courts, and an independent judiciary are essential safeguards. As Montesquieu famously wrote, “When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, or in the same body of magistrates, there can be no liberty.” But vetocracy is not simply about separating powers and protecting minority rights from the majority; it is about paralyzing democratic institutions and preventing the government from functioning.

Take the British example.

Businesses want a new high-speed railway, the company wants to invest in it, and even the government supports it. Yet an independent regulatory body, Natural England, can act as a veto player, imposing additional requirements and costs. And that is the key distinction Fukuyama discusses: the difference between constraints and capacity. Constraints are necessary because they protect our liberties from government overreach. But we also need government capacity: the ability to build things without being buried under thousands of regulations and a maze of supposed “independent actors” empowered by the state to obstruct or reverse policies.

These are the visible costs of regulation: the cancer hospital that cannot be expanded, the house that could help a young person get on the housing ladder, or the nuclear power station that could help bring down energy costs.

But the more serious costs are the ones unseen: the products that fail to come to fruition as a result of regulation. As the Austrian school economist Per Bylund has argued in his book “The Seen, the Unseen, and the Unrealized: How Regulations Affect Our Everyday Lives,” the problem with regulation is that it limits the possibilities of what could happen. It is not just about the direct financial cost of compliance. It is about the choices that disappear, the investments that never happen, and the economic freedom that is gradually eroded. The real cost of regulation is not only what we can see, but also what we never get to see because it was never built in the first place.

Vetocracy is a product of an overextended state: one that wants to be the dominant actor in the economy and micromanage every aspect of economic life.

Sooner or later, it discovers that governing is not as easy as it looks. The barriers originally created by the state in the name of better governance can make effective governance almost impossible. A vetocracy is a democracy that has accumulated so many opportunities to say no that it has lost the practical ability to say yes.

title: Why France?
desc:
Why France?

Authored by Stephen Soukup via American Greatness,

France is burning. But why? The obvious answer to that question is that it has imported massive numbers of people - often young, military-aged men - from parts of the world where violence is more prevalent. Or, as the President of the United States put it over the weekend, "The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country."

This is all well and good and, of course, there's a great deal to it. France has, indeed, "imported the third world" (to use the Vice President's phrasing). Interestingly, though, over the last couple of decades, France has imported far less of the Third World than its larger neighbors have, both in absolute and relative numbers.

Over the past ten years or so - since Third World immigration to Europe ceased to be a "problem" and became a "crisis" - no nation has seen a greater influx of foreign-born residents than Germany. From 2015 to 2024, Germany welcomed just over 6 million immigrants, which is equivalent to the rest of the EU combined. Its foreign-born population jumped from 13.4 percent to 20.9 percent, a massive increase, and the overwhelming majority of those immigrants came from "non-EU countries." The UK followed Germany with more than 4 million immigrants, and Spain was a slightly more distant third (in total number of immigrants).

Relatively speaking, Malta saw its foreign-born population jump from 9 percent in 2013 to 32 percent in 2024, the largest increase over the last decade (or so). It was followed by Luxembourg, Portugal, and Germany.

Compared with almost all of its European cousins, France's foreign-born population has increased relatively slowly, from 9.1 percent to 11.3 percent (albeit with a change in methodology). If the obvious answer were the correct answer, in other words, then Germany would be burning, Malta would be burning, the UK and Spain would be burning, but France would be fine. But it's not. So again, why is France burning?

I know that the consensus is that what is happening in France today is likely to happen in Germany tomorrow, the UK the day after that, and all across Europe next week. Moreover, the conventional wisdom on the Right has it that the French uprising should be seen as a warning to the United States, which is to say that all Western nations have similar problems to France and all Western nations should, therefore, be preparing to deal with domestic Third Worldism at some point in the not-so-distant future.

Now, to be fair, there is some truth in this. There are significant and universal problems associated with importing huge groups from non-Western societies and consciously choosing not to "Westernize" them or integrate them culturally. The West's crisis of confidence, its ideologically driven detestation of its own heritage, and its refusal to demand assimilation by its new residents are widespread failures that have produced and will continue to produce significant social, cultural, and economic issues. There can be little doubt about that.

At the same time, however, France is still different from the rest of us in the West. There is no real equivalent for the French experience - or at least there's no real equivalent in Europe.

For most of Europe, the "migrant crisis" began in 2015, when more than a million refugees from the Middle East and North Africa sought asylum from ongoing war and related devastation. For France, by contrast, its own migrant crisis started more than six decades earlier, in 1954, with the creation of the Algerian National Liberation Front (FLN), which issued a declaration calling for national independence on November 1 of that year and launched the Algerian Revolution/French-Algerian War. By the time the war technically ended eight years later, the Fourth French Republic had fallen, Paris police had massacred as many as several hundred Algerian immigrants in a single-day crackdown on dissent, tens of thousands of "harkis" - i.e., Muslim auxiliaries who fought for the French in Algeria - were resettled in France, and hundreds of thousands of economic refugees had fled Algeria for France (although some returned "rotationally"). Additionally, in 1968, six years after the end of the war, France and Algeria reached an agreement providing Algerians unique immigration and work status, which contributed to an approximate doubling of the Algerian population in France over the next 15 years.

What all of this means is that while France may have a lesser issue than its European brethren with a restless foreign-born population, it has a much more serious and much better-established problem with second- and third-generation immigrants, mostly from Africa. Those populations might not present a serious risk to the French state if they had been integrated in any serious or sustained way, but they haven't been. If anything, they've been rather mercilessly isolated and segregated from the productive parts of French society. When I wrote above that France has no equivalent in Europe, what I meant was that France's policies toward and treatment of its African migrants have a parallel of sorts, but one found, ironically enough, in Africa.

Two of the most significant and far-reaching acts of the National Party, the party of the Afrikaner white minority and the architect of apartheid in South Africa, were the 1959 Promotion of Bantu Self-Government Act and the 1970 Bantu Homelands Citizenship Act. Both of these were presented to the world as magnanimous acts on the part of the National Party to give the country's black population its own lands and a chance at political independence. In truth, of course, the Bantustans (literally "people places") were the apartheid regime's attempt to rid the white areas of the country of the black "surplus population" and to deprive them of their citizenship, thereby eliminating any claims they might someday make against their stolen property.

Black South Africans were divided up along rudimentary ethnic and linguistic lines and were then sent to the "homeland" that had been designated for their group. And when I say "sent," I mean that they were told to go, were given no choice in the matter, regardless of their connection to the land, and were then physically forced to move. Once in their new Bantustans, the people were told that they were no longer citizens of South Africa but were, instead, citizens of their new "homeland," which would be treated by the National Party regime as a "foreign" polity. In their generosity, the Afrikaners (that is to say, the descendants of the 17th- and 18th-century Dutch settlers) gave their black "former" countrymen 13 percent of the country's absolutely most craptastical land - even though blacks constituted roughly three-quarters of the population and even though the country is among the most blessed by God in terms of beauty and natural resources. Strangely, all the gold and the uranium and the rest of those resources just happened to be located in "white South Africa."

Anyway, the Bantustans served several purposes for the apartheid regime, but most significantly, they kept the black people where the government could keep an eye on them.

For much of the 1960s and 1970s, the French and South African governments remained on very good terms. France was apartheid South Africa's second-largest foreign partner and its collaborator in nuclear research and energy. Perhaps one of the things that bound the two regimes together was their mutual distrust of their "surplus populations," those undesirable foreigners, for whom they, apparently, had no use and no civil solution. That term, "undesirable foreigners," has its roots in the internments of the late 1930s and the Vichy years, when camps like Rivesaltes held those the state deemed unsuitable. As the historian of modern France Jeannette E. Miller notes, Rivesaltes was one of the more infamous of "the two hundred internment camps... that dotted the French countryside during the 'Dark Years,'" in part because it was "repurposed" by the post-war French government as a resettlement camp used to house harki immigrants. To be clear, the harki housing camps did not serve the same purpose as the Nazi transit camps, and they were not Bantustans, not even close. They were, however, brutal, ugly, depressing, and purposefully isolating. They were used by the French government to dispose of its unwelcome immigrants, the Algerians it felt a duty to resettle but whom it had no desire to integrate into French society.

These camps were also, in many ways, the antecedents to the nation's now-infamous banlieues.

Banlieues is a generic term identifying any suburb of any of France's major cities. But it's also a term that has been used more and more over the past couple of decades derogatorily, a term intended to convey the ugliness, poverty, and despair of the mostly African, mostly Muslim suburbs of Paris. These ghettos were created to be "utopias for workers," but, over time, came to be the place in which the descendants of African immigrants and other unwanted people are isolated. And they are almost entirely ignored by Parisian cosmopolitans - or at least they're mostly ignored, springing to mind only when their residents riot or commit acts of terror. The banlieues are where today's French keep their undesirables, their surplus population, the people whom they don't want to think about but would nevertheless like to keep an eye on. The banlieues are the places the French keep around because their minorities exist and, as Spike Milligan noted, everybody has to be somewhere.

For the last decade-plus, ever since the terror attacks at the offices of the satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo, American journalists have flocked to the banlieues to tell their story and to demonstrate their true beauty as hubs of "diversity." These journalists' real goal, of course, is to prove conservatives wrong about the banlieues being "no-go zones." What they've done in reality, however, is prove something else altogether: namely that France is a pretty screwed-up country and one flirting for years with the type of violence it's currently enduring. One such profile, penned by The New Yorker's George Packer, gives a good sense of the conditions:

Ben Ahmed, who is thirty-nine, works as a liaison between residents and the local government in Bondy - a suburb northeast of Paris, in an area called Department 93. For decades, a bastion of the old working class and the Communist Party, the 93 is now known for its residents of Arab and African origin. To many Parisians, the 93 signifies decayed housing projects, crime, unemployment, and Muslims. France has all kinds of suburbs, but the word for them, banlieues, has become pejorative, meaning slums dominated by immigrants. Inside the banlieues are the cités: colossal concrete housing projects built during the postwar decades, in the Brutalist style of Le Corbusier. Conceived as utopias for workers, they have become concentrations of poverty and social isolation....

For all their vitality, the banlieues feel isolated from the city, and from France itself. Parisians and tourists rarely visit them, and residents complain that journalists drop in only to report on car burnings and drug shootings.... Many suburban residents, meanwhile, never even think of going to Paris. Compared with American slums, the banlieues have relatively decent standards of housing and safety, but the psychological distance between the 93 and the Champs-Elysées can feel insuperable - much greater than that between the Bronx and Times Square. The apartment blocks in the cités, often arranged around a pharmacy, a convenience store, and a fast-food joint, look inward. Many have no street addresses, obvious points of entry, or places to park. The sense of separation is heightened by the names of the surrounding streets and schools, preserved from a historical France that has little connection to residents' lives....

To be clear (again), the banlieues are not Bantustans. Nothing else really could be; nothing else really could compare to the Nationalist South Africans' ingenious depravity. At the same time, though, the similarities are striking - and telling. Conservative commentators mocked Sky News over the weekend for attributing the violence in France to "economic inequality." That's fair, but only up to a point. There is undoubtedly a meaningful economic component to the anger and frustration exploding throughout the country. That's not the lone cause, of course, but it's not insignificant. As for the "inequality" variable, that too is important. As angry and violent as some black South Africans are with their white countrymen today, imagine how much more frustrated and violent they'd be if the free world hadn't applied the pressure necessary to overturn apartheid.

Now apply that to France.

The Western world is, indeed, at risk from importing masses of migrants who are unwilling to assimilate. Again, that much is clear. Still, the lesson to learn from France right now is that assimilation doesn't happen by accident. To save themselves, the nations and peoples of the West must recover their civilizational self-confidence and must, as a result, make a much greater effort to assimilate their newcomers and their children - economically and culturally.

title: US, Japan Begin Major Military Exercises Focused On Islands Near Taiwan
desc:
US, Japan Begin Major Military Exercises Focused On Islands Near Taiwan

Authored by Dave DeCamp via AntiWar.com

The US and Japan kicked off their biennial Keen Sword military exercise on Monday, one of the largest joint drills between the two countries. This year, the exercise will focus on Japan’s southwestern islands, including its westernmost island, Yonaguni, just 68 miles east of Taiwan.

Both the US and Japan have deployed new anti-ship missile systems to Yonaguni for the drills, ratcheting up tensions with China.

US Marines have been deployed with the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System, or NMESIS, which has a range of about 115 miles, putting vessels that patrol the coast of eastern Taiwan in range.

According to The Associated Press, Japan has deployed its first long-range Type-25 land-to-ship missile to the island. The Type-25 has a range of about 620 miles, making it capable of reaching mainland China from Yonaguni.

The US has also deployed a HIMARS rocket system to Ishigaki, about 150 miles from Taiwan, where the opening ceremony for Keen Sword took place.

HIMARS are capable of striking at a distance of up to 190 miles if they’re armed with the ATACMS missiles, but it’s unclear what type of ammunition the system was deployed with.

US Forces Japan said in a statement that the drill will involve 45,000 Japanese troops, 11,000 US troops, and forces from Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand, and the Philippines, along with observers from South Korea and the UK.

Song Zhongping, a Chinese military expert, told China's Global Times earlier this month that the deployment of a new US missile system in Yonaguni increases the risk of miscalculation between the US and China and that Beijing may respond by conducting its own military drills in the area.

The South China Morning Post previously reported that China has stepped up coast guard and naval activity east of Taiwan in response to maritime boundary talks announced in May between Japan and the Philippines.

title: Mexico Accuses Ex-Chihuahua Attorney General Of Treason For Letting US Agents Join Cartel Lab Raid
desc:
Mexico Accuses Ex-Chihuahua Attorney General Of Treason For Letting US Agents Join Cartel Lab Raid

Mexican federal prosecutors have accused a former state attorney general of treason for allowing US agents to join a drug-lab raid, and they arrested him again within hours of a state judge ordering him not to be jailed. Federal agents took Cesar Jauregui Moreno into custody after a Chihuahua court hearing ended Sunday night, and he is being taken to Mexico City to face a federal judge, with a transfer to the Altiplano prison, El Universal reported.

Federal Attorney General Ernestina Godoy announced the case Saturday in a video message, saying the investigation found he "may have engaged in conduct that could possibly constitute the crime of treason" by allegedly letting foreigners "take part in actions that correspond exclusively to national security forces," Reuters reported. Prosecutors allege he allowed US agents into an "irregular" April raid on a suspected drug laboratory without the authorization Mexican law requires. Jauregui has not been convicted of anything, and his defense argues the case is politically motivated.

The raid is the one that left two Americans dead. Between April 17 and 19, state and federal authorities dismantled a synthetic-drug lab in El Pinal, in the Sierra Tarahumara. On the way back, a vehicle went off the road and into a ravine, killing the state investigations chief, Pedro Roman Oseguera Cervantes, another state agent, and two Americans, Reforma reported. The Associated Press reported, citing a US official and two other people familiar with the matter, that the Americans worked for the CIA. The US Embassy had described them only as personnel "supporting Chihuahua state authorities' efforts to combat cartel operations," and the embassy, State Department and CIA declined to confirm the agency.

Jauregui said on April 20 that the Americans had not taken part in the operation, according to Reforma. Prosecutors later documented four foreign agents who accompanied Oseguera during it. Jauregui resigned on April 27, acknowledging "omissions" in the information and in institutional control, and was later questioned by federal prosecutors as a witness. Mexico News Daily reported that he and Governor Maru Campos both denied wrongdoing, and that President Claudia Sheinbaum said the CIA officers acted without the federal government's knowledge, which she called a violation of Mexican law.

The state prosecutor's case, separate from the federal treason charge, is where the fight played out last weekend. Reforma reported that the state charges are illegal exercise of public service and "coalition," and that prosecutors say Jauregui ordered and coordinated the participation of four US agents in the raid, then hid their presence at a press conference by saying they were there for drone training. They presented about 20 witnesses and a protected witness. Judge Luis Alberto Simental Ortega refused their request to close the hearing on national-security grounds and excluded testimony from Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former strategic-operations prosecutor who is himself a defendant with an arrest warrant out. Reforma said Jauregui told the judge he did not see the elements for the accusation against him.

The judge then refused to jail him before trial. Infobae reported that prosecutors argued he was a flight risk because of his foreign ties, and the judge answered that pretrial detention needs a specific justification and that his means alone did not show one. The conditions are surrendering his passport and US visa, signing in monthly and staying away from witnesses, and a hearing on whether to send the case to trial resumes Thursday, Oct. 22. Minutes after the ruling, Infobae said, the federal prosecutors served a treason warrant issued Saturday.

title: The Pope's Tweet And The Quiet Suicide Of Order
desc:
The Pope's Tweet And The Quiet Suicide Of Order

Authored by Kyle McClay via American Thinker,

On the World Day Against the Death Penalty, Pope Leo XIV posted a short statement that will be quoted by every abolitionist group in the country: the death penalty is "inadmissible" because it attacks the "inviolability and dignity of the person."

Effective detention, he insists, can protect society while still leaving the guilty a chance at redemption.

The timing was not accidental. It arrived the day after Vatican officials and U.S. bishops condemned the planned execution of Nidal Hasan, the Fort Hood jihadist who murdered thirteen soldiers and wounded dozens more in 2009.

Read the words again. The Pope is not arguing that Hasan is innocent, that the military court erred, or that the evidence was thin. He is arguing that the state should permanently warehouse a man who opened fire on unarmed troops in the name of jihad, and that this warehouse arrangement is somehow more consistent with human dignity than a public, final reckoning. That is not a theological refinement. It is a leadership failure with civilizational consequences.

Empires do not usually fall because barbarians suddenly appear at the gates. They fall because their own leaders lose the nerve to name evil, punish it in public, and thereby teach the next generation that certain lines are never crossed. When the highest moral authority in the West treats the execution of a mass murderer as an attack on dignity, ordinary people notice. Criminals notice. The next Nidal Hasan notices. The message is simple: the worst thing you can do to the community is still preferable to the worst thing the community can do to you.

For most of human history this was not a complicated question. Public execution was not a carnival of blood for its own sake. It was a deliberate spectacle of order. The condemned was brought before the community that he had injured. The sentence was read. The act was carried out in daylight. Citizens saw, with their own eyes, that the law was not a suggestion and that the victims had not been forgotten. Children learned the difference between the protected and the outlawed. Potential killers calculated the odds and often chose differently. The point was not sadism. The point was clarity.

Modern practice has inverted the arrangement. We hide executions behind concrete walls and chemical protocols while broadcasting every detail of the crime and the killer's childhood. We spend decades in appeals so that the original victims' families die of old age before the sentence is carried out.

We then congratulate ourselves on our refinement. Meanwhile, in cities that have effectively abandoned capital punishment and aggressive policing, the body count among the innocent continues. The people who pay the price are not the theologians writing about dignity from a safe distance. They are the soldiers at Fort Hood, the shopkeepers in high-crime neighborhoods, and the children who grow up learning that the state will protect the rights of the predator more carefully than it will protect them.

The claim that "effective systems of detention" can replace the death penalty for the worst offenders is an empirical assertion that has been tested. It fails. Determined killers continue to kill inside prisons. They order hits, radicalize others, and consume enormous resources. More important, the deterrent effect is diluted when the worst sanction is invisible and endlessly delayed. A respectable public execution -- orderly, solemn, conducted with the full procedural protections of the law -- restores the missing signal. It tells the community that its rules are real. It tells the next would-be mass killer that some acts place a person permanently outside the protection of ordinary life.

Pope Leo XIV's position continues the 2018 change in the Catechism under his predecessor. That change did not rest on new revelation. It rested on a judgment that modern states no longer need the death penalty and that the dignity of the guilty must be treated as co-equal with the dignity of their victims. That judgment has not been vindicated by the data on recidivism, prison violence, or the behavior of ideological killers. It has been vindicated only by the preferences of elites who rarely live with the consequences of the policies they recommend.

Bad leadership is not always dramatic. Sometimes it arrives as a short post about dignity that quietly tells the public the state will no longer do the hard, public work of justice. Empires that accept that message eventually discover that the people they refused to protect no longer believe the empire is worth defending. The remedy is not complicated. Restore the death penalty for the most aggravated murders. Carry it out in public, under law, with the gravity the crime deserves. Teach again that some acts end the offender's claim on the community's mercy. The alternative is the slow, respectable collapse the Pope's statement quietly invites.

desc:
US, Partners Seize Nearly 1,500 Pounds Of Cocaine In The Caribbean

Authored by Naveen Athrappully via The Epoch Times,

A U.S. task force and foreign partners seized nearly 1,500 pounds of cocaine in two operations in the Caribbean Sea over the past week.

The first interdiction involved U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) detecting a go-fast boat in the Caribbean, directing it to a port, and seizing about 562 pounds of cocaine, the Joint Interagency Task Force South said in an Oct. 15 post.

In the second interdiction, the Colombian Navy informed French Forces about another go-fast boat in the Caribbean Sea. One of the French frigates intercepted the vessel and seized roughly 917 pounds of cocaine, the Joint Interagency Task Force South said in an Oct. 16 post on X.

The Joint Interagency Task Force South's monitoring and detection efforts support U.S. Southern Command-led operations to dismantle narco-terrorist networks across the Eastern Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea. The task force is an international alliance of 13 domestic and 20 international partners.

The Caribbean is a "critical transshipment zone" for illegal drugs, mainly cocaine, according to a National Drug Control Strategy report issued by the White House. The region has a complex geography, with thousands of islands that offer ample cover for criminal groups to hide drug operations.

Criminal groups in the region use high-speed boats, submersibles, semi-submersibles, and low-profile vessels to transport cocaine, authorities said.

US Military Strikes

The Trump administration has been carrying out military strikes against suspected drug traffickers in the Caribbean and the Eastern Pacific for the past year. It has also designated several drug cartels and criminal groups as foreign terrorist organizations.

The administration has said that the vessels it struck were shipping narcotics that were ultimately headed to the United States.

Critics have said the military strikes are illegal. In an Oct. 14 statement, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) said that the attacks have killed at least 239 individuals since September last year.

The ACLU said that even if the vessels contained drugs, no international or domestic law authorizes using military force against criminal organizations, the advocacy group said, labeling the strikes as "premeditated killings of civilians" outside of an armed conflict scenario.

"We urge leaders in both Congress and the executive branch to finally end this illegal campaign before anyone else is killed," Jeff Stein, staff attorney with ACLU's National Security Project, said in the statement.

Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson justified the strikes in December last year, telling reporters that designated terror organizations operate the vessels.

The strikes have been thoroughly vetted by authorities and are aimed at defending American interests and protecting the country, Wilson said.

"Our operations in the Southcom region are lawful under both U.S. and international law, with all actions in compliance with the Law of Armed Conflict," Wilson said. "These actions have also been approved by the best military and civilian lawyers up and down the chain of command."

title: Hacker Copied Records Of Millions Of California Students Through Education Contractor ETS
desc:
Hacker Copied Records Of Millions Of California Students Through Education Contractor ETS

Authored by Kimberly Hayek via The Epoch Times,

The California Department of Education said Friday that a hacker accessed the data of millions of students by exploiting the system of a nonprofit contractor that works with the state. The data included students' names, birth dates, addresses, and disability status.

Educational Testing Service (ETS) began notifying students and families on Oct. 16 of the breach, which involved an unauthorized party using a compromised login to copy records from a secure file transfer site between May 22 and Sept. 18.

More than 5.7 million students were enrolled in California during the 2025-2026 school year.

"ETS takes the security of student information with the utmost seriousness, and sincerely regrets that this incident occurred," the department said in a statement.

The department is sending out ETS's Notice of Data Breach so families get details on the incident and available help. After learning of the breach, the department and the State Board of Education worked with state cybersecurity partners and ETS to assess what happened and prepare the notices.

ETS discovered unauthorized activity on Sept. 25 on a secure file-transfer site used to share California assessment data with the state. It disabled the account, took the site offline, and brought in outside cybersecurity experts.

Investigators found that someone used a compromised login to access the site and copy files at various times between May 22 and Sept. 18. The files covered California students, including those enrolled in the three previous school years.

Information that may have been copied includes student names, dates of birth, addresses, schools, grade levels, Statewide Student Identifiers, demographic details, disability and program participation status, and assessment records.

Social Security numbers, financial account information, passwords, and parent or guardian details were not involved.

The notice of data breach is available online in 27 languages on the California Department of Education website and provides additional details about the incident and the identity-protection services.

The department and the State Board of Education are reviewing the incident and ETS's compliance with applicable data security and contractual requirements. ETS has taken the old site offline and built a new one with stronger security controls. Regular monitoring has not found evidence that the information has been posted publicly.

California school systems have previously had data breaches. The cyberattack that hit the Los Angeles Unified School District in September 2022 involved hackers accessing about 2,000 sensitive student records.

A ransomware group stole a portion of the district's records and threatened to publish the information unless a ransom was paid. When superintendent Alberto Carvalho refused, the group published the data online weeks later.

Student data was stolen from the Long Beach Unified School District's records system and posted online, district officials said in an email to parents Feb. 22.

Information including student identification numbers, names, and email addresses was compromised, the district said in the email.

However, it noted that sensitive student and staff information, such as addresses, Social Security numbers, birthdates, and grades, was not compromised in the leak.

title: Bolivia's Energy Crisis Deepens As Natural Gas Reserves Run Dry
desc:
Bolivia's Energy Crisis Deepens As Natural Gas Reserves Run Dry

Authored by Felicity Bradstock via OilPrice,

  • Bolivia's dwindling natural gas reserves and declining exports have undermined its economy and intensified fuel shortages.
  • Rising global energy prices and subsidy cuts have increased living costs and fueled widespread protests.
  • A $1.9 billion IMF rescue package and energy-sector reforms aim to stabilize the economy, but long-term recovery requires diversification.

Years of underinvestment in Bolivia's gas industry have left the South American country facing a severe fuel shortage, as energy prices rise ever higher owing to the ongoing war in Iran. The energy shortages and economic crisis follow years of poor decision-making by the government.

In 2006, then-president Evo Morales took control of Bolivia's fossil fuel industry, renegotiating contracts with international oil and gas companies and benefiting from the revenue. Much of the country's newfound wealth was invested in public spending programs, expensive fuel subsidies, and the maintenance of a fixed currency exchange rate pegged to the U.S. dollar. Fossil fuel revenues contributed heavily to Bolivia's economy for several years, supporting GDP expansion and the development of social programs that helped halve poverty rates.

For many years, Bolivian's were led to believe that they had more extensive gas supplies than they actually did. However, in recent years, Bolivia's fossil fuel sector has suffered as reserves have dwindled and no successful gas discoveries have occurred. As of April, Bolivia has an estimated 3.7 trillion cubic feet of proven reserves. The fall in gas production led exports to fall by almost 60 percent over the last decade. Bolivia continues to rely heavily on natural gas, which accounts for around 70 percent of its electricity mix.

Meanwhile, little progress has been made in developing the country's green energy sector, leaving it facing severe energy shortages. The fall in gas revenues has left the economy suffering terribly, as inflation soars and the price of imported goods becomes ever more unaffordable. Luis Fernando Romero, the former head of an association of economists in southern Bolivia, stated, "We failed to take advantage of a historic opportunity that brought in immense revenue."

This situation is not uncommon, with many other oil-rich states having had similar experiences. Several Middle Eastern states have long depended on oil and gas revenues for economic growth, and most have only recently announced plans to diversify their economies to reduce reliance on fossil fuels. Several countries across the MENA region announced new economic strategies following greater talk of a global green transition, which could leave them missing out on vital oil revenues if they don't take moves to diversify and invest in value-added sectors.

The lack of investment in Bolivia's other domestic sectors has left it struggling to stay afloat as it runs out of fuel and is forced to pay high fuel import costs. President Rodrigo Paz warned that "International prices are forcing us to make complex choices."

In September, Bolivia's Congress approved a $1.9 billion loan from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), even though the terms of the deal require the government to impose strict austerity measures that could fuel social unrest. The loan received approval from the IMF's Executive Board on October 2, and the government will now be required to cut its fuel subsidies and significantly reduce public spending. It has already increased fuel prices and is expected to scrap further gasoline subsidies from the beginning of next year. The loan is expected to unlock up to $4 billion more in financing from the World Bank and other lenders.

However, there are major concerns that the new financial plan will significantly increase the cost of living for households already struggling. Last December, the government reduced fuel subsidies, leaving little support for the most vulnerable Bolivians. This led to widespread protests as people called for President Paz's resignation. In February, there was further social unrest after the distribution of poor-quality gasoline ruined thousands of vehicles. Then, in June and July, several weeks of road blockades by protesters occurred.

Meanwhile, to tackle the ongoing fuel shortages, Bolivia's government announced plans in September to triple the fund financing refined fuel purchases, following similar announcements by Peru and Ecuador. This is expected to help mitigate diesel shortages and rising prices. Both Peru and Ecuador have increased fuel subsidies in recent months and are focusing on increasing production at state oil refineries to alleviate the price pressure of expensive fuel imports.

In July, Bolivia's Energy Minister Marcelo Blanco announced that the government had authorized the private sector to import and sell refined fuels to mitigate severe shortages. Then, in September, the government said that the state hydrocarbons firm plans to focus on exploration, extraction, and refining to continue developing Bolivia's gas resources. However, experts warn that Bolivia could become a net fossil gas importer by around 2030.

As Bolivia continues to battle fuel shortages and seeks to support economic recovery by borrowing from international organizations, the government must focus on diversifying the economy by developing other value-added sectors to sustain long-term growth. In addition, the government must also develop Bolivia's renewable energy sources to reduce dependence on expensive fuel imports and ensure the country's energy security.

Authored by Tsvetana Paraskova via OilPrice,

Japan's average power prices jumped by over 25% at the start of this week from the previous week amid soaring LNG and higher coal prices.

The nationwide power price rose by over 25% week-to-week to $0.19 (31.15 Japanese yen) per kilowatt-hour (kWh) on Monday, Bloomberg reported, citing data from Japan Electric Power Exchange.

Japan, one of the world's biggest LNG importers, this summer reduced gas-fired generation in favor of coal as the price of liquefied natural gas remained elevated.

Japan has been burning more coal and less gas for power generation since the war in the Middle East started, and it is not the only one. All Asian countries have made the switch from gas to coal on affordability and availability grounds.

Moreover, surging oil prices have led to a significant increase in Japan's import bill for oil and LNG.

LNG prices surged in Asia to a four-year high as very few cargoes manage to exit the Strait of Hormuz while competition with Europe for winter supply is intensifying.

The average spot LNG price for delivery into north-east Asia in December was assessed at $29.30 per million British thermal units (MMBtu) at the end of last week. This was the highest spot LNG price for Asia since December 2022, and sharply higher compared to $26.50 per MMBtu assessed in the previous week.

As a result, Japan's gas-fueled power generation is the most expensive in years.

The switch to coal, for its part, has also had its cost challenges this year. Increased demand in Asia amid reduced supply from the top thermal coal exporter, Indonesia, is driving up coal prices, too. The global benchmark for coal prices, the Newcastle futures, have jumped by 30% compared to pre-war levels.

Power prices in Japan have also jumped this month due to scheduled maintenance at some power-generating facilities ahead of winter.

title: $270 Million In Suspicious Student Aid Fraud Flagged By Treasury
desc:
$270 Million In Suspicious Student Aid Fraud Flagged By Treasury

Authored by Naveen Athrappully via The Epoch Times,

The Department of the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has discovered roughly $270 million in suspicious financial activity likely associated with student aid program fraud.

FinCEN issued an alert in July asking financial institutions to report suspicious activities linked to student aid fraud.

A review of submitted reports identified more than 20,000 potentially suspicious transactions since February this year. FinCEN has reported approximately $270 million in suspected fraud to federal investigators for further investigation, the Treasury said in an Oct. 19 statement.

"Federal student aid is intended to expand educational opportunities, not line the pockets of fraudsters who steal from students pursuing their education and hardworking taxpayers," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in the statement.

"Treasury is working with financial institutions and law enforcement to identify these fraud schemes, recover stolen funds, and hold those responsible accountable."

The department said it was working with the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, headed by Vice President JD Vance, and encouraging whistleblowers to report fraud-related information.

In an example of educational fraud, the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced last month that a Detroit man was sentenced to 92 months in federal prison for fraud schemes, including one that targeted federal student aid programs.

The man and others submitted fraudulent student aid claims for more than 1,200 individuals, collecting more than $10 million before being caught, the DOJ said. The fraud spanned 100 schools across more than 20 states.

In March, the DOJ said a former professor admitted to stealing government funds through a scam involving fraudulent student financial aid applications. More than 100 such false applications were filed across several universities and colleges in Texas.

Education Aid Schemes

The Treasury detailed some of the federal student aid fraud schemes in its statement. For instance, "ghost student" schemes involve criminals stealing an individual's personal information and using it to enroll as a student in classes. The victim often never realizes that a third party is collecting student aid in their name.

In "straw student" schemes, fraudsters pay real people to enroll in classes and collect financial aid in their names. In some cases, corrupt school employees may be part of these schemes.

"Student aid fraud has real consequences for students and American taxpayers. It drains finite grant resources from deserving students, potentially prevents legitimate students from enrolling in classes occupied by fraudulent enrollees, and can leave identity theft victims responsible for debts they never incurred," the Treasury said.

In July, the Department of Education held a first-of-its-kind Higher Education Fraud Summit, with participants discussing ways to tackle fraud in the sector.

"We have already prevented nearly $2 billion in attempted federal student aid fraud from going to bad actors. Every dollar lost to fraud is a dollar taken away from a student trying to build a better future," Underssecretary of Education Nicholas Kent said in a statement.

In an October 2025 update, the University of Alaska warned students to protect themselves from student aid fraud. Specifically, the university said that students should share their personal information only with trusted, secure websites.

The university recommended that students regularly monitor their credit for any unusual or new activity and report any identity theft or other suspicious activity.

"Treat digital content, like emails, texts, voicemails, and website content, with increased scrutiny, especially if the materials or resources they provide or advertise seem too good to be true or appear designed to create a sense of urgency," the university said.

title: The Great Rare Earth Disconnect: Prices Up 23%, Miners Down 28%
desc:
The Great Rare Earth Disconnect: Prices Up 23%, Miners Down 28%

Here is a question that should be harder to answer than it is: China still controls the rare earth spigot, the latest Trump-Xi summit did nothing to loosen its grip, Japan is about to run out of yttrium, Washington has put a $110/kg floor under NdPr, and Western buyers are paying anywhere from 5x to 346x the Chinese price for heavy rare earths.

So why are rare earth stocks down on the year?

That is the question Canaccord's critical minerals team led by Reg Spencer asks in an overnight note titled "Rare Earths: Equity disconnect from strong market fundamentals", and the answer is blunt:

Given our favourable SxD outlook, floor pricing, recent pricing stability (NdPr), and Western pricing premiums (particularly for heavies), we think recent equity performance has been driven more so by global macro factors and highlights a disconnection from rare earth market fundamentals.

In other words, the commodity is acting like a strategic asset and the stocks are trading like a risk-off casualty. The numbers are stark: year to date, the ex-China NdPr price is up 23%, while Canaccord's rare earth developers are down 17% on average and its producers are down 28%.

We have been tracking the rare earth theme since long before China started rationing exports to the West in late 2024, and back in July 2025 we laid out "The Coming Rare Earth Revolution And How To Profit", flagging MP Materials as the stock best positioned to benefit. A few hours later the Pentagon announced its MP deal, and well we allowed ourselves a modest victory lap:

Last night we said MP is the stock best positioned to capitalize on the rare earth revolution. Up 43% this morning

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) July 10, 2025

Fifteen months later, MP trades at $40.17, about half of Canaccord's $82 target. So what happened?

The Chart That Says It All

Canaccord's chart below shows the problem in one picture. Chinese NdPr (black) and Rotterdam NdPr (dark blue) have converged and climbed steadily all year, with the Western price now above $110/kg. Meanwhile the REMX ETF (light blue) peaked in May and has since slid from above $100 to the high-$50s.

The carnage is broad. On the producer side, Lynas, MP, USA Rare Earth and Iluka are all deep in the red, and even China Northern Rare Earth and Shenghe are lower on the year. Diversification at its finest.

Developers did a bit better on average, mostly thanks to Viridis (VMM), which is still up well over 50% on the year. Strip that out and the picture is grim: Hastings is down roughly two-thirds, St George about half, and Arafura and Brazilian Rare Earths 35-50%.

Canaccord's verdict: "We question how equities have performed so poorly YTD despite strong underlying market fundamentals." Those fundamentals include recent sector M&A, direct government support, a scarcity of Western supply and "ex-China NdPr pricing up 23% YTD."

The Floor Works... Just Ask China

Start with the most important structural change of the past year. As we reported when the Department of Defense set a price floor last August, Washington has moved from financing Western supply to underwriting its economics. Canaccord tallies the floors: US$110/kg NdPr for MP (DoD), Lynas (Japan, US, plus upside sharing) and USA Rare Earth, which also gets US$575/kg for dysprosium and US$2,050/kg for terbium.

And the floor has done something nobody expected: it has tamed the Chinese price too. For years Beijing used export quotas, policy changes and, more recently, export controls to whipsaw NdPr from about $175/kg down to around $50 and back again. Over the past 10 months, Canaccord notes, Chinese pricing has "begun to normalise around the US$110/kg floor price level."

Put differently, the volatility that made rare earth projects unbankable has largely vanished, and yet investors are paying less for those projects than they did in January.

Two Markets, Two Prices

NdPr is now a one-price market, more or less. Everything heavier is a different story. Since Beijing started rationing heavies, the West has developed its own (thin, opaque) price for anything China won't ship, and the gaps are absurd. Rotterdam dysprosium sits around $1,074/kg vs $227 in China, and terbium at $4,594 vs $983.

But Dy and Tb are the tame ones. Canaccord now forecasts yttrium, gadolinium and samarium for the first time, and the Western premiums there are almost comical. Chinese yttrium oxide has averaged about $8/kg over the past five years, while European spot is "~US$740/kg", a premium of 85x, and "some price reporting agencies have quoted US prices of up to US$1,750/kg." Gadolinium trades about 10x China in Baltimore, with US CIF quotes as high as $3,100/kg.

We ran Canaccord's own spot price table through the calculator, and here is what the "dual market" looks like element by element. CIF North America samarium, used in the SmCo magnets that go into missiles, fighter jets and radar, trades at 346 TIMES THE CHINESE PRICE!

And the squeeze is very real. Just this morning the FT reported that Japan has made an urgent request to Washington and global companies to help resolve its yttrium crisis, warning of a severe shortage by year-end. "Inventories are plummeting," one official said. Per Argus, yttrium oxide costs about $9/kg in China and roughly $1,150/kg outside it, a 179-fold jump in two years. A senior US official added that China is shipping the US just two-thirds of the rare earths it promised under last October's truce, and Japan "only the bare minimum." That followed last month's Trump-Xi summit, where China pledged to buy US coal but fell short on rare earths, and the two sides settled for a two-month truce that markets promptly faded.

To be fair, Canaccord is careful here. It notes the ex-China DyTb market was just 151 tonnes in 2025, and China's was 22x larger. It warns that Western premiums "should be viewed cautiously" and that "we question whether pricing is sustainable at these levels," with some magnet makers already pivoting to lower-cost ferrite magnets. Its own price deck has ex-China yttrium falling from $740/kg this year to $100 by 2030. Still, even the bank's haircut numbers leave Western producers with integrated separation (it names Lynas and MP) earning premiums nobody would have modeled two years ago.

Demand Goes Up, Again

Meanwhile the demand side keeps getting revised higher. Canaccord now sees NdFeB magnet demand growing at a 7.3% CAGR to ~365,000 tonnes by 2035, 15% above its prior update. EVs remain the anchor (52 million units by 2035 vs 23.5 million in 2026), but the bank has added data centers (motors for cooling), e-bikes and scooters, and drones. Drones are only ~1% of forecast demand, but the bank notes that Ukrainian and Russian military drone production alone was estimated at ~9 million units, so "our model forecasts may prove conservative."

Then there are the robots. Canaccord models humanoid deliveries growing at a 45% CAGR to 2.5 million units by 2035, and points out that Tesla is reportedly preparing an Optimus line designed for 1 million robots a year. For comparison, global EV sales rose more than 4,600% from 2014 to 2024. Maybe the robot curve won't look like that... but if it does, the magnet math gets very ugly very quickly.

Netting it all out, Canaccord sees the global NdPr market in deficit through 2028 (about 7% short this year), roughly balanced in 2029-31 as Eneabba, Kangankunde, Caldeira, White Mesa and the Lynas expansions come online, and then sliding back into a deeper deficit: -10% by 2035. Dy+Tb follows the same shape, ending at a 12% deficit.

The West's Blind Spot

The bulls' case gets even stronger once you look past the mines. Canaccord forecasts ex-China NdFeB magnet capacity rising more than 300% by 2030 to about 70,000 tonnes, which sounds impressive until you realize it would still be only 23% of global capacity, with China at ~77%.

And the West may not even get there, because it is missing a step. Global NdFeB metallisation and alloying capacity is about 210,000 tonnes in 2026, and more than 90% of it is Chinese controlled. Ex-China capacity is set to roughly double to 38,000 tonnes by 2030, which falls well short of planned Western magnet capacity. Canaccord calls metallisation "a major blind spot in western supply chain development", and its channel checks found lead times of up to two years for strip casters, "with sourcing from China impossible under current export controls."

This echoes ING's warning, which we covered two weeks ago, that China's rare earth chokehold may outlast this decade because the bottleneck is "industrial rather than geological." Canaccord's conclusion is just as stark: "our research points to China maintaining market dominance, with shortfalls in Western supply (and likelihood of ongoing Chinese export controls) supporting bifurcated markets and pricing premiums."

Translation: the scarcity premium for anything mined, separated or metallised outside China is a structural feature that will be around for years, and the companies capturing it are trading as if it will be gone by next quarter.

Wall Street Is Paying 50 Cents On The Dollar

Which brings us to valuation. Canaccord's producer coverage trades at an average 0.57x P/NAV and its developers at 0.47x. On the bank's targets, MP has 104% upside, Lynas 108% (target raised to A$23), USA Rare Earth 204% and Energy Fuels 150%, even after Canaccord cut its EFR target to C$30 on project delays.

The rating changes: Meteoric (MEI) goes to Hold from Spec Buy, since its value is now tied to Lynas' all-scrip takeover at 0.0207 LYC shares per MEI share. (Lynas shares fell almost 8% the day that deal was announced, another reminder that this market keeps punishing consolidation.) Hastings (HAS) goes to Spec Buy from Hold "on valuation", even though its target was cut to A$0.30 from A$0.55, which tells you just how far the stock has fallen.

Of course, price targets have a habit of following prices rather than leading them, and at least some of the selloff has a perfectly sensible explanation: these are long-duration, capex-heavy projects at a time when the 10Y is above 5%, tech is wobbling and the bid for anything speculative has evaporated. Canaccord concedes as much, blaming "global macroeconomic pressures."

Same Disconnect, Different Metal

Tungsten isn't a rare earth, but it is a critical material with the same chokepoint (China controls roughly 80% of supply, per Jefferies), and it shows the exact same disconnect, only worse. Take Almonty Industries (ALM), the most prominent Western tungsten miner and a name we have covered extensively in recent weeks.

When Goldman's Nick Cash initiated coverage last month, he put Almonty "at the center of the Western tungsten investment narrative," with tungsten prices up 8x since the start of 2025. He was also the Street's skeptic, expecting prices to normalize and Sangdong's ramp to run slower than the market hoped, with a $13 target vs a $24.73 consensus. The stock was $12.74 that morning. Today it is below $9, down 62% from its April peak and back where it started the year, after dropping another 10% on the day of yesterday's Investor Day. So even Goldman's cautious target now implies about 45% upside.

Meanwhile the operations are going the right way. Sangdong in South Korea started production in September and is moving toward 24/7 operations, with its first concentrate shipment due later this month, and Cantor's Matthew O'Keefe models output jumping from 126,287 MTU this year to 444,400 MTU in 2027, with all-in sustaining costs falling from $905 to $319 per MTU. Oppenheimer's Ian Zaffino puts the shares at just 5.7x/4.2x FY27/FY28 EBITDA, with roughly $290 million in net cash.

So what spooked the market? Spot prices. Western APT has slipped from $3,140 to about $2,700/MTU, and Chinese prices have retreated even more sharply. But Zaffino explains why that is a misleading signal: Western APT and oxide plants are running at capacity under long-term contracts and can't absorb more concentrate, so "concentrate prices have softened, even as availability of finished APT/oxide in the West remains constrained." And the demand wave hasn't even started. On January 1, 2027, US defense procurement rules extend to tungsten mining, refining and separation, so Chinese or Russian ore processed in a third country no longer qualifies. Stifel says the US strategic tungsten stockpile is nearly depleted, and Bernstein sees the Western rearmament order boom running from 2027 through 2030. The cherry on top: on Monday, CME announced plans to launch tungsten futures by early Q1 2027 at the latest (subject to regulatory review), which tells you how seriously the market's plumbing is taking a metal that equity investors are currently dumping.

In other words, spot is pricing today's bottleneck in Western processing, and the stock is pricing spot, while the 2027 demand cliff is priced almost nowhere. Sound familiar?

Supply Security Gets The Stage In London

Goldman, for its part, thinks the debate has already shifted. Its third Global Metals & Mining Conference kicks off in London today during LME Week, bringing together the world's largest "diversified, copper, aluminium, rare earth and lithium producers." In their conference preview, Goldman's Matt Greene and the bank's mining team write that "the conversation has increasingly shifted to supply," with governments "becoming more active participants in the mining sector through faster permitting, shared infrastructure, strategic funding, price floors and direct offtake agreements, reflecting the growing importance of resource security." The question the bank poses is the right one: "whether the industry can deliver the supply that markets are increasingly pricing in."

For rare earths, the honest answer seems to be: not anytime soon, and not without China. Which is exactly why the sector's stocks probably shouldn't be trading at half of NAV.

When Macro Lets Go

We have seen this movie before. Back in March we reported that the US reportedly had just two months of rare earths left, and in July that China's "killer chokepoint" was reshaping the global economy. Each time the physical market tightened, and when Washington finally stepped in (see last July's MP deal), the equities caught up violently.

Today we have a two-month trade truce that expires January 10, a Japanese government begging for yttrium, the West's flagship tungsten miner trading below even Goldman's skeptical target ten weeks before the Pentagon's sourcing rules kick in,a floor price that has turned NdPr into a one-way bet with a safety net, and an equity market that is valuing the West's only scalable non-Chinese suppliers at roughly half of what they're worth on conservative assumptions.

Canaccord's closing line sums it up: "We expect demand to remain strong, as the West looks to secure ex-China supply and build its independence within the global magnet supply chain."

Our take: the disconnect will probably close the same way it did last summer, with a headline out of Beijing or the Pentagon, and the investors waiting for macro to give them the all-clear will be buying it 50% higher. After all, nothing cures a 0.5x P/NAV like a 346x price premium.
