desc:
"A Good Idea": SpaceX Jumps On Blowout Quarter, Musk Confirms Committees Discussing Tesla Merger

Update (1730ET): The earnings call has seen SPCX shares extend their after-hours gains amid a tsunami of attention-grabbing comments from Elon Musk and CFO Bret Johnsen.

Perhaps the most shocking was Musk saying that he sees between $500 billion and $1 trillion of annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027.

Then he stepped it up further:

Musk says there’s a small opportunity for SpaceX to have 20 gigawatts of AI compute online next year.

Musk says he’s been spending a lot of his time in Memphis, "often four days a week," trying to get more data center compute developed.

He’s aiming to bring in 13 gigawatts of compute by the end of next year.

And this year, he expects between 2.5 GW and 3 GW to come online.

As a reminder, (based on this quarter’s numbers) they have 1.7 GW of nameplate compute.

“We are, frankly, hounded relentlessly by every hyperscaler,” Musk says, referring to demand for SpaceX data centers.

“I don’t think we’re going to have a demand issue here.”

And finally, the topic of merging Tesla and SpaceX was brought up:

"I'm tap dancing through a minefield," says Musk on the question of a merger, adding that both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss this idea.

Musk also downplayed the move somewhat:

"“I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it."

But then he adds:

"I do think there’s a lot of merit for combining the companies," Musk says, concluding that "I think it will be a good idea".

The market is pricing a 66% chance of the merger being completed by the end of next year...

All of that combined, has pushed SPCX up around 5%...

* * *

As we wrote in our preview, hopes are high for what SpaceX will report today. The company is expected to report solid revenue growth, however more than offset by far more solid capex growth which will result in SpaceX burning almost a quarter trillion over the next 3 years as it builds out its data center capacity. Notably, SpaceX could post its first quarterly profit today - though this is only its second earnings report as a public company. Wall Street expects earnings of 15 cents a share, or about $1.9 billion in net income, compared with a $541 million loss last quarter.

Besides the top and FCF lines, Deutsche's list of "other areas of focus" is a good checklist of what else to look for:

  • AI: neocloud pricing and new contracts, the Cursor contribution, Grok Bot adoption, and the data center capex outlook (read: any hint that 2027 capex starts with a "2").
  • Launch: timing of the next few launches after Flight 14; Flight 15 looks set for mid-/late November, though DB doesn't expect a second-stage catch.
  • Connectivity: after the $8 billion Grain spectrum deal, "additional color on management's next move(s) in the US (build vs. buy)," which is something the wireless carriers will be listening to closely.

Additionally, investors are seeking additional hints about a potential Tesla and SpaceX merger. Today’s earnings are happening just a few days after Tesla unveiled its new Roadster, which incorporated SpaceX gas thrusters that allowed the vehicle to hover and do barrel rolls in the air. Following the event, a bunch of Tesla and SpaceX executives and employees started following each other on X, according to an account that monitors tech executives. DB said that the timing as "mainly a function of valuation differentials and politics (may want to avoid a potential Democrat-led administration taking over post Trump)."

Elon Musk has talked a lot about the “convergence” of his businesses over the last year. Meanwhile SpaceX and Tesla are already collaborating on one of Musk’s most ambitious projects: the Terafab, which aims to mass produce semiconductor chips in the US to be used in his companies’ various products.

Don't expect to see much, if any profit: Starlink satellite-internet service is SpaceX’s only profitable business. The militarized version of Starlink, called Starshield, came under increased scrutiny last week after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the White House and Musk of placing restrictions on the technology in Ukraine, disrupting military operations. Both Musk and Trump have denied involvement, igniting a firestorm over who controls the technology that has become indispensable to Ukraine’s war against Russia.

As for the market's reaction, recall that SPCX shares slumped 14% the day after its first earnings release in August, in part over fears that insiders would sell shares after the earliest of many lockup expirations. Those fears were quickly calmed when the shares rebounded, but the setup heading into this quarter’s results is similar to last time. On Wednesday, an additional 1.3 billion shares, representing 28% of those subject to the 180-day lock-up period, will become available to trade.

So with all that in mind, here is what SpaceX just reported for Q3, its second quarter as a public company. For the most part a solid beat across the board, blowing past Wall Street expectations, and posting its first quarterly profit, $4.4 billion, or 35 cents a share, more than double estimates, while spending a massive $20 billion on capex

  • Revenue $14.58 billion, beating estimates of $12.87 billion
    • Space revenue $1.77 billion, beating estimates of $1.43 billion
    • Connectivity revenue $5.25 billion, beating estimates of $4.86 billion

Here is the revenue by segment: it shows that SpaceX is no longer a Rocket Company but is now mostly a neocloud, pardon, Hyperscaler.

  • Capital expenditure $19.59 billion, beating estimates of $19.6 billion
    • Space capital expenditure $1.61 billion, higher than estimates of $1.52 billion
    • Connectivity capital expenditure $1.54 billion, below estimates of $1.6 billion

Here is the capex by segment:

Turning to expenses...

  • Total Costs & Expenses $11.78 billion, beating estimates of $11.23 billion
  • R&D expenses $4.60 billion, missing estimates of $5.06 billion

... and operating income:

  • Operating income $2.79 billion, beating estimates of $2.24 billion
  • Connectivity operating income $2.37 billion, beating estimates of $1.86 billion
  • Adjusted Ebitda $8.81 billion, smashing estimates of $6.59 billion
    • Space adjusted Ebitda $357 million, estimate $123.1 million
    • Connectivity adjusted Ebitda $3.50 billion, estimate $2.94 billion

Here is the adjusted EBITDA by segment:

  • Number of rocket launches 35, missing estimates of 41
  • Mass to Orbit 476 mt, missing estimates of 559
  • Cash and cash equivalents $51.29 billion, estimate$91.2 billion

While much will be said about the company's profitability, note that the $4.4 billion of net income got a boost from $1 billion of “other income” and a $390 million tax benefit. That said, the underlying business still beat expectations: operating income was $2.8 billion versus $2.2 billion expected.

A visual way of representing what happened in Q3:

Looking at the key components, EBITDA and CapEx, we find that both revenue and EBITDA smashed estimates, while CapEx was largely unchanged from last quarter.

As we noted in our preview the big question would be the delta between EBITDA and CapEx growth, and as shown in the chart below, while EBITDA was a record $8.8BN, it is still nowhere near enough to catch up to the whopping $19.6BN in capex.

Another very important number: amount of installed compute rose to 1.7GW, just shy of estimates of 1.74GW.

Summarizing the fine print: SpaceX reported blowout revenues and EBITDA, driven by stronger ARPU, even as ending compute, consumer broadband subs and external launches all came below expectations.

Commenting on the quarter, the SpaceX CFO said that the company "delivered another strong quarter in Q3. Revenue grew an impressive 161% year-over-year, fueled by continued momentum in Connectivity and a clear inflection in our Super Intelligence business. The combination of our launch leadership, recurring Starlink revenue, and the significant expansion of our SI infrastructure continues to drive meaningful operating leverage... We are building the infrastructure of the future with discipline — focused on capital efficiency, strong returns on invested capital, and maintaining a robust, investment-grade balance sheet — while moving with the velocity to capture the opportunity in front of us."

In its wrap, Bloomberg writes that SpaceX of this quarter is not the same as the SpaceX of last quarter. AI - now officially called Super Intelligence - has overtaken Starlink to become the company’s biggest business by revenue. Just last quarter, Starlink was comfortably ahead. The speed of that shift shows just how quickly SpaceX’s AI infrastructure business is scaling.

The SpaceX story used to be rockets funding satellites. Increasingly, it’s rockets, satellites and a giant balance sheet funding an AI company. In other words, a hyperscaler.

The results were solid, and the stock liked them - at least until the call - with SPCX stock higher about 3%, fading a bit of its after hours jump.

title: The Deep(er) Midterms
desc:
The Deep(er) Midterms

Authored by Victor Davis Hanson via American Greatness,

There are two ways of looking at the midterms, now less than three weeks away.

title: US Nears Russia Deal To Free Detained Americans, Witkoff En Route To Moscow
desc:
US Nears Russia Deal To Free Detained Americans, Witkoff En Route To Moscow

ABC and The New York Times are reporting that multiple Americans detained in Russia could soon be free as part of a major Trump deal with Moscow.

Negotiations are said to be in the final stages, with Special Envoy Steve Witkoff set to be in Moscow on Wednesday. And so a major announcement and release could happen by the time he leaves the Russian capital later the same day.

Stephen Hubbard, an American who is accused of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine forces when he was captured in 2022, is expected to be among the released prisoners.

Citing unnamed officials, ABC writes, "They add that the talks have centered on freeing Stephen Hubbard, a 72-year-old retired teacher who is the only American held in Russia officially designated as wrongfully detained by the State Department, as well as several other U.S. citizens held by Moscow on what the administration said it believes are dubious charges."

President Trump acknowledged Monday that he was "trying to get a hostage that the country has been after for a long time" - which appeared to refer to Hubbard. "Let's see what happens," Trump said. "That'll be soon."

On Tuesday, Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky met in Oslo as part of efforts to find an end to the Ukraine war. In a closing presser for the talks, Zelensky said the latest working proposal features security guarantees for Ukraine modelled on NATO's Article 5, which is the collective defense clause.

"We have discussed security guarantees, and I’m grateful to the American side for emphasizing once again that they will be strong," Zelensky said following talks in Oslo.

"We discussed NATO, Article 5 and Article 5-like guarantees. Different types of security guarantees are included in the document, which Steve will share with the Russians, and we will hear their feedback."

However, the Kremlin is unlikely to go for NATO Article 5-style protections, given a key rationale for the 'special military operation' in the first place was NATO expansion up to Russia's doorstep.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has meanwhile said, "We hope that a meeting can be arranged in the very near future, and that the American negotiators, Mr. Witkoff, will be able to brief President Putin on their contacts with both the Ukrainians and the Europeans."

Norwegian PM Jonas Gahr Store says US envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to St Petersburg tomorrow for talks with the Russian leadership, following today’s discussions in Oslo with Zelensky and EU representative Alexander Stubb. “He will... exchange ideas from this meeting and proposals developed by European and American colleagues, and possibly pave the way for a meeting at the leaders’ level.”

— Brian McDonald (@BrianMcDonaldIE) October 20, 2026

Witkoff is due in Moscow Wednesday, where he is indeed expected to present the results of the Oslo talks to Putin and his team.

Peskov said further: "We consider such meetings to be of great importance on every occasion. They are always timely and very substantive, and we greatly appreciate the mediation efforts of the American negotiators."

title: When The Normals Say Enough Is Enough
desc:
When The Normals Say Enough Is Enough

Authored by Silvio Canto, Jr. via American Thinker,

Remember the kid in school who was always negative and complaining about everything? I usually avoided that kid, and maybe voters are starting to turn off all of this political anger, too. I think they call it “fatigue” as Scott McKay points out:

I was at lunch Wednesday with one of my non-political friends, and — as often happens, and I swear I’m not the one driving this — a topic of conversation turned political.

My friend brought up an exhausting pattern which, we agreed, is ramping up in both volume and frequency. Namely, that we as a society are jumping from one unhinged rage to another over things which don’t justify the level of vitriol and over-emotional screeching they’ve produced.

Four of these factored prominently in the conversation, but a fuller picture could include several more. Just this year we had the Renee Good fiasco, the Lindsay Clancy trial, the Cornell 7 orgy controversy, and now the Shane Gillis-gymgirl dustup.

My friend noted that in all of these cases — and, again, there have been several others — it’s generally women who have gotten most torqued up about the topic at hand, and in particular it’s a certain subset of women who are doing it. And TikTok and Instagram are full of rage-bait videos of people going berserk over things which either don’t merit such a reaction or where the truth is a whole lot more complicated than they’d like to make it.

And it was my friend, and not me, who suggested that none of these moral panics are organic, and that this burgeoning rage engine has already exhausted normal folks.

I think my friend is probably right. Outrage fatigue is a real thing. I think outrage fatigue played a role in Donald Trump’s 2024 election — though it was the fatigue normal folks had over the cultural aggressions of the radicals in society.

Whether it was Drag Queen Story Hour or trans kids or Tren de Aragua or the abuse of the FBI or countless other things demoralizing them, the normals had enough — and didn’t care what the aggressors had to say about how horrible a person Trump is.

As a normal guy, who loves politics and to share opinions, I understand that we have reached a point where all of this political rage is not normal.

Once upon a time, I would get together with friends for lunch and our rage was about the umpire who missed too many pitches last night.

Once in a while, a friend was angry because his girl got upset because he wouldn’t answer her text in 30 seconds.

Or another time, a guy was mad because the apartments wouldn’t fix the AC on time. The normal stuff to get angry about.

Today, there is always someone at the table who wants to convince us that Trump is a threat to democracy and will cancel the elections.

He becomes obnoxious when he won’t shut up or keeps sending negative texts about Trump.

Most of us keep reminding him that our lunch is to talk about real stuff, not just Trump. He can’t let go.

Trump is Hitler, you know, and came to power by winning an election.

Where is all of this going?

I don’t know for sure, but I do think this fatigue is real. It’s one of the reasons that people are keeping their politics private, not putting political signs in their yard, and not talking to pollsters.

Furthermore, I hear from single guys that they avoid certain women who are just too political no matter how nice they look in jeans. And I hear from young men that they are dating girls from other countries because American college girls are just too political. As one said recently, I don’t go on a date to argue about Roe v. Wade!

Maybe normals like me have had enough with all of this rage! Or maybe some need to go see a psychiatrist and get Trump out of their heads.

title: SpaceX Jumps On Blowout Quarter As AI Sends Revenue, EBITDA Soaring
desc:
SpaceX Jumps On Blowout Quarter As AI Sends Revenue, EBITDA Soaring

As we wrote in our preview, hopes are high for what SpaceX will report today. The company is expected to report solid revenue growth, however more than offset by far more solid capex growth which will result in SpaceX burning almost a quarter trillion over the next 3 years as it builds out its data center capacity. Notably, SpaceX could post its first quarterly profit today - though this is only its second earnings report as a public company. Wall Street expects earnings of 15 cents a share, or about $1.9 billion in net income, compared with a $541 million loss last quarter.

Besides the top and FCF lines, Deutsche's list of "other areas of focus" is a good checklist of what else to look for:

  • AI: neocloud pricing and new contracts, the Cursor contribution, Grok Bot adoption, and the data center capex outlook (read: any hint that 2027 capex starts with a "2").
  • Launch: timing of the next few launches after Flight 14; Flight 15 looks set for mid-/late November, though DB doesn't expect a second-stage catch.
  • Connectivity: after the $8 billion Grain spectrum deal, "additional color on management's next move(s) in the US (build vs. buy)," which is something the wireless carriers will be listening to closely.

Additionally, investors are seeking additional hints about a potential Tesla and SpaceX merger. Today’s earnings are happening just a few days after Tesla unveiled its new Roadster, which incorporated SpaceX gas thrusters that allowed the vehicle to hover and do barrel rolls in the air. Following the event, a bunch of Tesla and SpaceX executives and employees started following each other on X, according to an account that monitors tech executives. DB said that the timing as "mainly a function of valuation differentials and politics (may want to avoid a potential Democrat-led administration taking over post Trump)."

Elon Musk has talked a lot about the “convergence” of his businesses over the last year. Meanwhile SpaceX and Tesla are already collaborating on one of Musk’s most ambitious projects: the Terafab, which aims to mass produce semiconductor chips in the US to be used in his companies’ various products.

Don't expect to see much, if any profit: Starlink satellite-internet service is SpaceX’s only profitable business. The militarized version of Starlink, called Starshield, came under increased scrutiny last week after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the White House and Musk of placing restrictions on the technology in Ukraine, disrupting military operations. Both Musk and Trump have denied involvement, igniting a firestorm over who controls the technology that has become indispensable to Ukraine’s war against Russia.

As for the market's reaction, recall that SPCX shares slumped 14% the day after its first earnings release in August, in part over fears that insiders would sell shares after the earliest of many lockup expirations. Those fears were quickly calmed when the shares rebounded, but the setup heading into this quarter’s results is similar to last time. On Wednesday, an additional 1.3 billion shares, representing 28% of those subject to the 180-day lock-up period, will become available to trade.

So with all that in mind, here is what SpaceX just reported for Q3, its second quarter as a public company. For the most part a solid beat across the board, blowing past Wall Street expectations, and posting its first quarterly profit, $4.4 billion, or 35 cents a share, more than double estimates, while spending a massive $20 billion on capex

  • Revenue $14.58 billion, beating estimates of $12.87 billion
    • Space revenue $1.77 billion, beating estimates of $1.43 billion
    • Connectivity revenue $5.25 billion, beating estimates of $4.86 billion

Here is the revenue by segment: it shows that SpaceX is no longer a Rocket Company but is now mostly a neocloud, pardon, Hyperscaler.

  • Capital expenditure $19.59 billion, beating estimates of $19.6 billion
    • Space capital expenditure $1.61 billion, higher than estimates of $1.52 billion
    • Connectivity capital expenditure $1.54 billion, below estimates of $1.6 billion

Here is the capex by segment:

Turning to expenses...

  • Total Costs & Expenses $11.78 billion, beating estimates of $11.23 billion
  • R&D expenses $4.60 billion, missing estimates of $5.06 billion

... and operating income:

  • Operating income $2.79 billion, beating estimates of $2.24 billion
  • Connectivity operating income $2.37 billion, beating estimates of $1.86 billion
  • Adjusted Ebitda $8.81 billion, smashing estimates of $6.59 billion
    • Space adjusted Ebitda $357 million, estimate $123.1 million
    • Connectivity adjusted Ebitda $3.50 billion, estimate $2.94 billion

Here is the adjusted EBITDA by segment:

  • Number of rocket launches 35, missing estimates of 41
  • Mass to Orbit 476 mt, missing estimates of 559
  • Cash and cash equivalents $51.29 billion, estimate$91.2 billion

While much will be said about the company's profitability, note that the $4.4 billion of net income got a boost from $1 billion of “other income” and a $390 million tax benefit. That said, the underlying business still beat expectations: operating income was $2.8 billion versus $2.2 billion expected.

A visual way of representing what happened in Q3:

Looking at the key components, EBITDA and CapEx, we find that both revenue and EBITDA smashed estimates, while CapEx was largely unchanged from last quarter.

As we noted in our preview the big question would be the delta between EBITDA and CapEx growth, and as shown in the chart below, while EBITDA was a record $8.8BN, it is still nowhere near enough to catch up to the whopping $19.6BN in capex.

Another very important number: amount of installed compute rose to 1.7GW, just shy of estimates of 1.74GW.

Summarizing the fine print: SpaceX reported blowout revenues and EBITDA, driven by stronger ARPU, even as ending compute, consumer broadband subs and external launches all came below expectations.

Commenting on the quarter, the SpaceX CFO said that the company "delivered another strong quarter in Q3. Revenue grew an impressive 161% year-over-year, fueled by continued momentum in Connectivity and a clear inflection in our Super Intelligence business. The combination of our launch leadership, recurring Starlink revenue, and the significant expansion of our SI infrastructure continues to drive meaningful operating leverage... We are building the infrastructure of the future with discipline — focused on capital efficiency, strong returns on invested capital, and maintaining a robust, investment-grade balance sheet — while moving with the velocity to capture the opportunity in front of us."

In its wrap, Bloomberg writes that SpaceX of this quarter is not the same as the SpaceX of last quarter. AI - now officially called Super Intelligence - has overtaken Starlink to become the company’s biggest business by revenue. Just last quarter, Starlink was comfortably ahead. The speed of that shift shows just how quickly SpaceX’s AI infrastructure business is scaling.

The SpaceX story used to be rockets funding satellites. Increasingly, it’s rockets, satellites and a giant balance sheet funding an AI company. In other words, a hyperscaler.

The results were solid, and the stock liked them - at least until the call - with SPCX stock higher about 3%, fading a bit of its after hours jump.

title: Anthropic's Updated S-1: An $80.7BN Half-Year Loss, A $750BN Compute-Tab, And A 'Catastrophic Incident' Warning
desc:
Anthropic's Updated S-1: An $80.7BN Half-Year Loss, A $750BN Compute-Tab, And A 'Catastrophic Incident' Warning

Three weeks ago, when the first leaked draft of Anthropic’s confidential IPO prospectus made the rounds, we noted that CEO Dario Amodei was preparing to take the company public at the exact moment the underlying math of the frontier AI trade had begun to turn against him. That September filing showed a company that burned through $42 billion in net losses during 2025 on just $4.6 billion in revenue, sitting on $20 billion in cash while staring down $518 billion in long-term compute commitments.

On Tuesday, The Wall Street Journal reviewed a more recent draft of Anthropic’s S-1 registration statement covering the first half of 2026. Every headline number has moved substantially higher – and none of the structural flaws have been fixed.

In the six months ended June 30, 2026, Anthropic generated roughly $16.3 billion in revenue, up from $1.1 billion in the year-earlier period and more than triple the $4.6 billion it generated in all of 2025. Yet across that same six-month window, Anthropic recorded a staggering $80.7 billion net loss – up from $13 billion in the first half of 2025, nearly double its full-year 2025 deficit, and one of the largest half-year corporate losses ever committed to paper.

Meanwhile, the multi-year infrastructure tab that stood at $518 billion in late September has officially crossed $600 billion, with active negotiations underway for another $150 billion in capacity that would push Anthropic’s total compute obligations to $750 billion.

Metric Full-Year 2025 (Sept. S-1 Leak) 1H 2026 (Updated Oct. S-1 Draft) Latest Trajectory & Context
Revenue $4.6 Billion $16.3 Billion ~$4.8B in Q1; ~$11.5B in Q2; $16.8B in Q3
Compute & Infra Spend $7.3 Billion ~$9.0 Billion Up from $2.3B in 1H 2025; already exceeds all of 2025
GAAP Net Loss $42.0 Billion $80.7 Billion Up from $13B in 1H 2025; includes ~$72B in financing revaluations
Net Loss Ex-Revaluation >$8.0 Billion (Operating Loss) ~$8.7 Billion Underlying burn running at a ~$17B+ annualized clip
Contracted Compute Tab $518 Billion >$600 Billion Negotiating up to $150B more (up to $750B total)
Customer Concentration High Enterprise Reliance 20% from 2 Customers Many large buyers lack long-term contracts

The $80.7 Billion Loss – And What Lies Beneath The Accounting Charge

To be sure, bulls and syndicate bankers will immediately point out that roughly $72 billion of Anthropic’s $80.7 billion first-half loss is a non-cash accounting artifact. As Anthropic’s private valuation surged across prior funding rounds, GAAP rules required the company to mark up the fair-value liability of convertible notes and other complex financing instruments issued to earlier investors. Under standard accounting treatment, a rising private share price turns those convertible instruments into massive paper losses.

Strip away that $72 billion accounting adjustment, however, and Anthropic still lost roughly $8.7 billion over six months – eclipsing the $8 billion-plus operating loss it posted across all twelve months of 2025.

The culprit is straightforward: direct compute and infrastructure spending hit nearly $9 billion in the first half of 2026 alone, up nearly fourfold from $2.3 billion in the first half of 2025 and surpassing the $7.3 billion Anthropic spent on compute for the entirety of last year. Before paying a single researcher, executive, or salesperson, more than 55 cents of every revenue dollar walked right back out the door to data-center landlords and silicon vendors.

The $750 Billion Take-Or-Pay Escalator

As we detailed in August ("The Teaser Period: Why The AI Boom Is Hitting A Reset Wall"), the defining feature of the AI infrastructure buildout is the quiet transformation of cloud computing from a flexible, pay-as-you-go operating expense into a rigid, noncancelable debt structure.

Anthropic’s updated S-1 is the ultimate case study in that transition. According to the filing, the company is now on the hook for roughly $450 billion in cloud computing contracts over the next seven to ten years. Crucially, the prospectus notes that the bulk of these agreements are noncancelable and must be paid "regardless of actual usage." Those commitments include:

  • $111 billion contracted with Google Cloud

  • $110 billion contracted with Amazon Web Services (AWS)

  • $31 billion contracted with Microsoft

  • Up to $86 billion to rent Nvidia chips from smaller AI cloud providers Nscale and Lambda through 2033 and 2034, respectively

Layer on top of that more than $160 billion in obligations to lease Google TPU chips through a separate arrangement with Broadcom, and Anthropic’s locked-in infrastructure bill exceeds $600 billion – before counting the additional $150 billion in compute deals the company is actively negotiating. And as we reported earlier ("Forget CDOs, Meet CCOs: This Isn't A Tech Cycle... It's 2008 With Silicon"), that contractual mountain sits alongside tens of billions of dollars in off-balance-sheet chip-lease arrangements financed through special-purpose vehicles (SPVs) and private-credit facilities.

Yet even $600 billion to $750 billion isn't buying security of supply. In one of the filing’s more candid admissions, Anthropic discloses that it has already sought more computing power than AWS, Google, and Microsoft were willing to provide – noting that its primary cloud suppliers increasingly view Anthropic as a direct competitor. Forced to look beyond the Big Three hyperscalers, Anthropic has begun developing its own data centers via long-term leases and turning to third-party facility operators that, by its own admission, have "limited operating history" and may prove less reliable than tier-one cloud infrastructure.

The Fatal Duration Mismatch: 10-Year Liabilities vs. 2 Fickle Customers

In the legacy cloud era, multi-year data-center backlogs were underwritten against the diversified, recurring cash flows of tens of thousands of profitable Fortune 500 companies. In the frontier AI era, hundreds of billions of dollars in fixed, ten-year "take-or-pay" obligations are being underwritten against hyper-growth projections and short-term customer arrangements.

Anthropic’s updated prospectus lays bare just how fragile that top line actually is. Roughly one-fifth (20 percent) of Anthropic’s $16.3 billion in first-half revenue – or about $3.26 billion – came from just two customers. Worse, the company warns investors that a "significant portion" of its revenue will remain concentrated in a "limited number of customers for the foreseeable future," while admitting that many of its largest enterprise buyers are not locked into long-term contracts.

Consider the balance-sheet mismatch public equity investors are being asked to swallow:

  1. On the liability side: $600 billion to $750 billion in seven-to-ten-year, noncancelable take-or-pay compute obligations that convert from "booked compute" to "billed compute" on a fixed schedule, utterly indifferent to end-market demand.
  2. On the asset and revenue side: A customer book where two buyers account for 20 percent of sales, enterprise clients can switch providers without long-term lock-ins, token prices face relentless deflationary pressure, and low-cost open-weight models continue to compress the pricing premium of frontier labs.

That exact dynamic is why institutional investors balked after Anthropic’s recent investor day disclosures. As we noted last week, management touted third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion, an 11 percent adjusted operating margin for a second consecutive quarter, and positive free cash flow.

What spooked the room wasn't the absolute figure – it was the slope. With first-half revenue at $16.3 billion and second-quarter revenue at roughly $11.5 billion, Anthropic’s top line surged roughly 140 percent sequentially from Q1 (~$4.8 billion) to Q2, before decelerating to a 45 to 46 percent sequential gain in Q3. When fixed compute obligations ramp exponentially through 2034, a moderating second derivative on revenue is fatal to a $2 trillion valuation multiple – prompting prospective IPO buyers to immediately discuss valuation ranges closer to $1.5 trillion.

Blackmailing Models, Uninsurable Catastrophes, And The "Public Benefit" Shield

Roughly one-third of the entire draft prospectus is devoted to risk factors, reading less like a software registration statement and more like a containment protocol mixed with a legal disclaimer.

Anthropic explicitly warns prospective shareholders that its AI models can exhibit "self-preserving" behaviors to avoid being shut down and may generate responses that resemble "blackmail" in an attempt to convince human operators to keep them online. Because the company bears direct liability for certain harmful model behaviors – ranging from stolen data to severe security incidents – it faces massive financial exposure. And if a model triggers what the filing calls a "catastrophic AI-related incident," Anthropic warns that the resulting damages could be so large that it would be unable to obtain commercial insurance to cover the liability.

Compound that with growing physical-world friction – Anthropic flags that political resistance to data-center construction has "become more organized and coordinated across jurisdictions" and that its public profile "may draw particular attention to projects associated with us," forcing it to sign letters of intent for capacity outside the United States – and the governance picture grows even murkier.

Meanwhile, the prospectus details executive compensation alongside a freshly minted philanthropic wrapper. Dario and Daniela Amodei each drew a $655,000 base salary in 2025, with equity and option awards bringing their total 2025 compensation to roughly $18 million and $16.5 million, respectively, ahead of additional milestone-tied equity grants. Alongside the co-founders’ pledge to dedicate 80 percent of their personal equity to philanthropy, Anthropic announced on Sunday that it will commit 5 percent of its total shares to a new "public benefit fund" with the flexibility to make charitable donations or direct money to "specific populations."

For retail and institutional buyers alike, the proposition could hardly be clearer. Public shareholders are being invited to absorb 5 percent upfront share dilution for a public benefit fund, assume uninsurable liability for self-preserving AI models, rely on two uncontracted customers for a fifth of top-line revenue, and backstop up to $750 billion in non-cancelable, ten-year compute leases – all so venture insiders and hyperscaler landlords can convert off-balance-sheet IOUs into public-market liquidity before the growth curve flattens out.

title: CME Plans World's First Tungsten Futures As Booming Missile Demand May Spark Severe 2030 Shortage
desc:
CME Plans World's First Tungsten Futures As Booming Missile Demand May Spark Severe 2030 Shortage

CME Group plans to launch the first tungsten futures contract as deepening resource nationalism, Chinese export restrictions, and rising demand from the global rearmament cycle intensify Western governments' focus on securing conflict-free materials and highlight the industrial base's urgent need to hedge future price risk. These new contracts would introduce exchange-traded forward pricing to a market that currently relies heavily on spot prices and has limited visibility into future pricing.

Trading is expected to begin in early 1Q27, subject to regulatory review. The contract will be settled against Fastmarkets' Western benchmark for ammonium paratungstate, or APT, the raw material and commercial precursor for almost all downstream tungsten products.

For miners, manufacturers, and trading desks, the potential benefits extend well beyond hedging. A liquid futures curve could show how the market participants view the worsening global supply constraints for the critical metal. That would add a new forward-looking dimension to spot prices, allowing participants greater visibility into pricing months and years out.

"Tungsten sits at the intersection of advanced manufacturing, semiconductor technologies and geopolitics, and our clients are increasingly seeking to hedge their exposure and improve price transparency," said Jin Hennig, CME Group's managing director and global head of metals.

"CME Group Tungsten futures will join our growing suite of critical minerals and energy transition metal products, providing clients more opportunities to manage risk as global supply chains restructure," Hennig added.

Fastmarkets CEO Raju Daswani pointed out, "Growing volatility and concentrated supply are increasing the need for transparent, trusted price benchmarks in the tungsten market," adding, "The launch of this contract, based on Fastmarkets' tungsten APT assessment, is a significant step in the market's development, connecting physical-market price discovery with new opportunities to manage price risk."

Fastmarkets' Western APT benchmark surged after China, in early 2025, restricted the flow of the critical metal to Western defense and industrial companies, sending prices as high as $3,000 a ton. Spot prices have since moved lower to around $2,775.

CME's announcement coincided with Almonty Industries' Investor Day at Nasdaq in Midtown Manhattan, where the tungsten producer presented to analysts from Oppenheimer, Stifel, Jefferies, Goldman Sachs, and other firms.

CEO Lewis Black and the management team outlined a constructive operating outlook for the miner's South Korean, Spanish, and Portuguese mines, along with updates on expansion projects and additional supply sources.

Almonty's investment case centers around its move to be one of the largest conflict-free tungsten miners (ex-China) for the West. Its operating assets and expansion pipeline position the miner as a tungsten lifeline for the rearmament cycle.

Black told investors that constrained Western tungsten supplies are strengthening Almonty's commercial position, supporting improved offtake terms as Sangdong ramps Phase 1 production and advances its Phase 2 expansion.

Sangdong's Phase I is designed to process 640,000 tons of ore annually. Phase II is planned to double that capacity, with equipment ordering and underground planning already underway.

Several projects offer additional growth potential:

  • Rwanda: A planned joint venture, to be owned 75% by Almonty and 25% by the government, would initially source and process material from local producers. Management views this as a faster route to incremental supply while longer-term mining projects advance.
  • Panasqueira: Drilling for the Portuguese mine's Level 4 expansion is expected to finish by year-end. Management is also evaluating the recovery of tungsten and other metals from existing tailings.
  • Los Santos: Tailings processing has produced encouraging laboratory and pilot results, supported by an offtake agreement with a price floor. Commercial viability remains unproven.
  • Montana: Existing permits and nearby infrastructure support development potential, but detailed planning remains underway. The presentation did not establish a firm production timetable.
  • Sangdong molybdenum: Additional drilling is intended to validate historical data and support an updated technical report, providing a separate development opportunity beneath the tungsten deposit.

"Almonty remains one of the key solutions to meeting western tungsten demand after China's exit from the market and the company's impressive production ramp is still unfolding with prices just off record highs. We are updating our target price to $21 given the push-out of Sangdong shipments but remain Buy rated," Stifel materials analyst Brock Cannon wrote in a note after the investor meeting.

Jefferies chemicals and materials analyst Laurence Alexander said the Sangdong ramp remains a near-term catalyst. He indicated that the early January ban on US defense companies sourcing tungsten from foreign adversaries or conflict areas "represents a clear pivot point in demand, which should align favorably with the Sangdong production ramp."

Alexander continued, "The US will prohibit defense contractors from acquiring tungsten, tungsten metal powder, and tungsten heavy alloys mined, refined, or produced in China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea. With only ~13% of global production from conflict-free zones, the qualified supply pool is likely smaller than the headline deficit implies. Should a similar EU measure be implemented, Western premiums likely widen further."

The key takeaway from the new CME contracts, set to begin trading early next year, is a forward curve that will provide the first clear view of how the market interprets the shortage of this critical material.

A Financial Times story published overnight adds to the mounting global news coverage, suggesting that spot prices for critical materials remain disconnected from reality, as China's resource nationalism has left Japan just "months" away from "running out of critical rare earths."

We'll leave readers with the most impactful chart from Almonty's investor deck, presented to analysts yesterday. It shows a widening structural tungsten deficit emerging around 2030.

In that case, it's all about "owning the bottlenecks." The mining sector has been de-rated in the second half of the year, but it will bottom out at some point, and the theme of owning the top producers will reemerge amid the rearmament cycle ramping up.

He summons the town to City Hall, removes the helmet, and reveals himself as Apu. "I am the man you left for dead. I am the one you pretended never existed," he declares.

The character is now voiced by India-born, U.S.-raised actor Sunil Malhotra, known for animation work including The Legend of Korra and The Legend of Vox Machina.

In the episode, Apu recounts being dumped on the Island of Forgotten Garbage, healed by Dr. Nick, returning home to find his family and the Kwik-E-Mart gone, and then being ignored by everyone in town as if invisible.

Marge steps in with language that tracks the show's own earlier hesitation: "Apu, we're so sorry we left you for dead. Believe me, we wanted to do the right thing." Bart adds, "But we were so scared, and just didn't know what to do."

Homer offers a penance that doubles as a reminder of the character's previous place in town life: "You were on our bowling teams, our barbershop quartets, our dad rock cover bands. We took you for granted. I took you for granted." The sequence turns out to be a nightmare; Apu wakes in the Kwik-E-Mart with Manjula (now voiced by Janina Gavankar) and agrees to attend a Halloween party.

Showrunner Matt Selman described the approach as deliberate. "We love this character, and wanted to bring him back in a smart, 'Simpsons'-y way that allowed him to evolve," he told Variety. "We're excited by what Sunil has already brought to the role, and look forward to seeing more of Apu in the future."

Viewers who watched the episode did not share that enthusiasm. Reactions on X described the new voice as try-hard and the character as louder and much less appealing than the version that had been retired.

title: Voters More Worried About Iran War Than Immigration Or Crime: Polls
desc:
Voters More Worried About Iran War Than Immigration Or Crime: Polls

Authored by Blaise Malley via Responsible Statecraft,

As election day nears, two new polls show the Iran war has emerged as one of the most important issues shaping voters' midterm decisions.

National polls from Fox News and The Associated Press-NORC place the war behind only economy-related issues, government corruption, and health care among voters' top four concerns.

Significantly, the Iran war has surpassed immigration and crime, two issues on which President Donald Trump performed particularly well in 2024, among voters' top concerns. In the 2024 campaign, pre- and post-election polling showed those issues as ranking higher as a priority for voters than foreign policy.

The Fox News survey showed 75% of respondents were either "extremely" (42%) or "very" (33%) concerned about the war in Iran. According to the AP-NORC poll, 62% of registered voters named the war as one of the most important issues, and a further 31% said it was "an important issue, but not one of the most important."

The Fox poll further found that six in 10 voters oppose U.S. military action against Iran, and those voters favor Democratic congressional candidates by 56 points.

Some of the specific economic concerns voters mentioned, including gas prices and the cost of living, have been driven by an energy crisis fueled by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, blurring the line between economic and foreign-policy concerns.

Both polls were conducted in roughly the same window. AP-NORC surveyed 1,119 adults, including 925 registered voters, between Oct. 8-12 , with a 3.9-point margin of error, while Fox surveyed 1,202 registered voters Oct. 9-12, with a 2.5-point margin of error.

Many election analysts have compared this midterm election to that of 2006, when the combination of an unpopular war in the Middle East and economic frustration at home helped deliver that year's Democratic wave, in which the party gained six Senate seats and 31 seats in the House.

As Jim Antle of the Washington Examiner wrote in RS this week, "today, the public has even less patience for the current war than in 2006."

In addition to the war's importance to respondents, the polling also indicates that voters are souring on Trump, and his foreign policy.

The AP-NORC poll shows a mere 33% approval rating for the president's foreign policy, the lowest that percentage has been across eight polls by the same firm during Trump's second term. The 35% approval rating for Trump's foreign policy in the Fox News poll is similarly the lowest recorded by Fox since his return to office.

Republican candidates across the country have certainly noticed. In tight races in Michigan, Maine, Iowa, and elsewhere, Republican nominees have called for a swift end to the war, though some maintain that this can still be accomplished militarily.

In leaked private audio reported by Axios earlier this month, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate for Senate, admitted that his campaign's primary problems were driven largely by the war in Iran and its effect on gas prices.

On Tuesday, Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-Wis.), who is running for governor of his state, said it was time to "wrap up" the war.

"The president is doing what he believes is best for the United States of America," Tiffany said. "What I'm focused on is being the best governor possible in Wisconsin."

title: Don't Let The Fed Steal Your Kids' Future
desc:
Don't Let The Fed Steal Your Kids' Future

Authored by George Ford Smith via Mises Institute,

The Federal Reserve's inflation machine not only disrupts our lives now, but it also is making life even for difficult for those facing an uncertain future...

My grandson is 21, pursuing a degree in college and active in sports and social life. His future looks bright. But he and others of his generation will enter that future with a handicap imposed on them by people they have never met: Policymakers at the Federal Reserve. They claim to be "firmly committed to fulfilling its statutory mandate from Congress of promoting maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates."

What's wrong with that? In Fed parlance "stable prices" mean prices that remain roughly the same. As a government-created central bank that manages the nation's monetary system, the Fed calls 2 percent inflation over the longer run "price stability." But 2 percent inflation does not mean stable prices, it means prices approximately double over 35 years.

And, since the Fed rarely if ever hits the 2 percent target, CPI calculations based on government historical data show prices increasing at a much higher rate. More importantly for a government so attracted to war, the Fed will always shelve its 2 percent target to feed government's hawkish appetite.

Yes, Fed monetary managers are fallible, one could argue. They're well-educated and experienced, but they still err. Aren't they doing the best they can, given their unwritten partnership with government?

But the relevant question is: Are they necessary? Milton Friedman's paper "Monetary Policy: Theory and Practice," published in the Journal of Money, Credit, and Banking on February 14, 1982, says loud and clear they are not.

If a domestic money consists of a commodity, a pure gold standard or cowrie bead standard, the principles of monetary policy are very simple. There aren't any. The commodity money takes care of itself.

Friedman, strangely, did not conclude from this that we should simply return to a classical gold standard. He famously criticized commodity standards partly because maintaining them consumes real resources - labor and capital devoted to mining and storing monetary gold. He generally favored fiat money governed by rules, apparently forgetting that rules in government hands are never hard and fast but always subject to expediency.

Economics as a Neutral Science

Gary North, in his 2016 essay, "The Moral Issue of "Honest Money," explores Friedman's objections to gold. He begins by criticizing economics as "neutral," as unconcerned with moral issues. What does a morally neutral viewpoint look like?

"If the Nazis wish to exterminate 50,000 people, which are the most cost-effective means?" No morality, you understand, just simple economic analysis. The problem with the theory of neutral economics is that people are not neutral, effects of government policies are not neutral, social systems are not neutral, legal systems are not neutral, and when pressed, even economists are not neutral.

Most people, and this "includes virtually all Ph.D.-holding, card-carrying economists," believe public confidence and not gold is what matters most in monetary affairs. But the contractual right to redeem gold (or silver) for the promised metal spelled out on the face of the commodity substitute (a warehouse receipt) is the public's way of guarding their guardians and ensuring the public's trust. Let's not forget:

Government and its licensed agents have a monopoly of money creation. Private competitors are called counterfeiters.

Bitcoin partially achieves competitive status as a store of value because of its cap at roughly 21 bitcoin. No FOMC decides to increase that ceiling because unemployment rises, banks fail, or the government needs to fund another war.

If the government issues currency such as have today - without a promise of redemption - the public can only rely on government-established means such as elections to govern their "public servants." But elections are not contracts. A politician promising peace if elected is under no obligation to pursue peace, as Americans have seen especially since 1917.

There are, of course, constitutional mechanisms other than elections for controlling federal officials: separation of powers, judicial review, impeachment, congressional investigations, appropriations, and, ultimately, constitutional amendment. A president or other civil officer can be impeached by the House and removed after a two-thirds Senate conviction. A member of Congress can be expelled, but that requires a two-thirds vote of the member's own chamber.

But notice the difference from redemption. Under the old convertibility arrangement, someone dissatisfied with the currency didn't have to persuade 51 percent of the electorate or bear the cost of a lawsuit. He could say, in effect: "I don't trust your paper. Give me the gold you promised."

North's criticism of Friedman rests on a confirmation of the latter's objections, given the restrictions that a gold standard imposes on government. North begins:

It is quite true, as Milton Friedman has stated so graphically, that the gold standard is expensive. We dig gold out of the ground in one location, only to bury it in the ground in another location. We cannot do this for free. Wouldn't it be more efficient, meaning less wasteful of scarce economic resources, Dr. Friedman asks, just to forget about digging up gold? Why not keep the government or the central bank from expanding the money supply? Then the same ends could be accomplished so much less wastefully. Save resources: trust politicians.

But this is not the whole story.

By tying the currency unit to that gold - which is wonderfully expensive to mine, as any monetary brake should be and must be - the body politic enlists a cadre of professional, self-interested speculators to serve as an unpaid police force. This police force polices the trustworthiness of government monetary promises.

The public can relax, knowing that a hard core of greedy capitalists is at work for the public interest, monitoring Federal budgets, Federal Reserve policies, and similarly arcane topics. By forcing the Treasury to "go long" in its own promises market, the guardians are guarded by the best guards of all: future-predicting, self-interested speculators whose job it is to embarrass those who do not honor contracts - their own contracts.

Conclusion

Government is not just force, but a legal monopoly of superior force. When that monopoly expanded to money as it did with the Federal Reserve Act of 1913, government started a ball rolling in our direction that intentionally siphons purchasing power from our currency.

Fiat money depends on Fed-government restraint. That restraint loosens as world crises develop. Since fiat money feeds the crises, the prospects for restraint are anyone's guess.

The money you earn is yours. A monetary system based on gold, unencumbered by government manipulation, helps you keep it by protecting its purchasing power. People just starting out in life, such as my grandson, would do well to understand that principle - especially when our present fiat system falls apart.
